title: Full Section A text pair: The Bakery at Four and The Bakehouse
subject: English Language
source: Written for english-language/y10 lesson 56 (Full Section A text pair 'The Bakery at Four' (Text One, modern) and 'The Bakehouse' (Text Two, in a nineteenth-century style), teacher-written (pupil PDF))
intro: Lesson 56. Reading stamina: a full Section A. Read both texts, then answer Q1 to Q6 in 30 minutes.

passage.title: Text One: The Bakery at Four
paras: At four in the morning the bakery on Mill Street is the only lit window for half a mile. Inside, Mrs Rahman has already been working for an hour. Flour hangs in the air like fine snow. The ovens tick as they heat. By six the first loaves come out, cracking softly as they cool, and the queue begins: night-shift workers, a bus driver, two nurses. Nobody hurries. Mrs Rahman slips an extra roll into the bag of the old man who pays in coins. 'Bread,' she tells me, 'is the first kindness of the day.'

passage.title: Text Two: The Bakehouse
paras: I was admitted to the bakehouse below the street a little before dawn, and confess I have never known such heat. The men worked stripped to their shirts, their arms white to the elbow, and the great oven glowed like the mouth of a furnace. They had begun at midnight and would not rest till noon. Yet when a ragged boy put his face to the grating, the master baker, a stern and silent man, broke a warm loaf in two and passed half up through the bars without a word. I thought it the most eloquent speech I heard in London.

questions.q: Q1. By what time do the first loaves come out?
Q2. What does the flour hang in the air like?
Q3. How does the writer use language and structure to present the bakery?
questions.a: The lit window as a beacon ('the only lit window for half a mile'); flour 'like fine snow' (calm, beauty); the ticking ovens and loaves 'cracking softly'; the list of night workers in the queue; 'Nobody hurries.'; the extra roll; the closing quotation 'the first kindness of the day'; the time structure from four to six.

questions.q: Q4. When had the men in Text Two begun work?
Q5. Give two things the writer tells us about the conditions in the bakehouse.
questions.a: Any two: intense heat; men stripped to their shirts; arms white with flour; the oven glowed like a furnace; work from midnight till noon.

questions.q: Q6. How does the writer use language and structure to present the master baker's act?
questions.a: 'confess' (personal, daring); the furnace simile (hellish heat); the 'stern and silent' baker set against his silent gift; the bars and grating (poverty, separation); the paradox of the 'most eloquent speech' made without words.

questions.q: Before the timer: note one link between the texts for Q7
questions.a: For example: kindness to the poor: the extra roll and the half loaf passed through the bars.

questions.q: Core (timed, 30 minutes): read both texts and answer Q1 to Q6 in the portal
questions.a: 1) six (o'clock). 2) fine snow. 3) points: the lit window as a beacon ('the only lit window for half a mile'); simile of flour 'like fine snow' (calm, beauty); sounds of ticking ovens and loaves 'cracking softly'; the list of night workers in the queue; 'Nobody hurries.'; the extra roll; closing quotation 'the first kindness of the day'; time structure four to six. 4) at midnight. 5) any two: intense heat; men stripped to their shirts; arms white with flour; oven glowed like a furnace; work from midnight till noon. 6) points: 'confess' (personal, daring); furnace simile (hellish heat); contrast of the 'stern and silent' baker with his silent gift; the bars and grating (poverty, separation); paradox of the 'most eloquent speech' made without words.

Stretch: if time remains, check every quotation is short and embedded

options: read both texts, then Q1 to Q6 in order to the time plan
Q6 first, then read Text One
